entries.title: Discovery work starts again to find absent histories
paragraphs: We started the project again to find histories absent from the first event list. The new search starts with places and periods with fewer atlas cases. Each case needs a real source location before review. Open leads stay visible. This method makes no claim that the atlas covers all history.

entries.title: Research review: a missed Pacific history
paragraphs: The search beyond the first list found its first case that completed research review. It is about the conquest of Lau by Maʻafu from 1852 to 1869. The case stays out of the public atlas and active data set. Its record has three phases and 29 unknown fields. Separate Mago and Munia or Yanuyanu questions do not have decisions.

entries.title: Research review: Florida mission destruction
paragraphs: The second case beyond the first list has a research review. It is about attacks on Florida mission communities from 1702 to 1706. The case is not in the public atlas or active data set. One count says the attacks took about 1,000 captives. The record does not use the later Seminole name for those older groups.

entries.title: New public case: Equatorial Guinea
paragraphs: The live atlas now has the Macías Nguema dictatorship and mass exile from Equatorial Guinea from 1968 to 1979. The case is about political flight, blocked return, and children born in exile. It gives each estimate with its date. The source does not confirm claims of forced plantation labor. This release has 530 cases across 540 playback stops.

entries.title: New public case: Sierra Leone
paragraphs: We added the Sierra Leone case, from 1991 to 2002. It is about flight in the civil war. The text has details on flight within the state and refuge across borders. It also has details on return and flight after return. Commission statement counts are not totals for all people. This release has 531 cases and 541 playback stops.

entries.title: New public case: Beni and nearby Ituri villages
paragraphs: The live atlas now has a case on attacks in Beni Territory and nearby Ituri villages from January to 19 March 2021. The case reports an estimate of 40,000 newly displaced people. This estimate does not include people displaced before the attacks or the deaths. We do not know the routes, return, or long-term land results. This release has 532 cases and 542 playback stops.

links.label: Open the Beni and Ituri case

entries.title: New public case: Zanzibar property confiscation
paragraphs: The latest live atlas has a case on state seizure and transfer of property in Zanzibar from 1964 through September 1987. The source counts 1,565 properties. That number does not count people or households. The case does not use seized property as proof of expulsion, and questions about removal are open. This release has 533 cases and 543 stops. Another 79 known cases need text, and 64 cases have evidence or classification holds.

entries.title: Sixty research topics have two searches
paragraphs: We used two separate search methods for 60 topics across regions, periods, and processes. The searches found candidates in 24 topics. The searches found no candidates in 19 topics within the stated limits. Sources or access did not permit complete searches for 17 topics. Another 1,220 topics still need both searches. The search program is still open.

entries.title: More population and region records
paragraphs: All 676 source events now use one standard world region label. The population index now has stable records for 177 named groups. It has 343 links from groups to events. It also has five supported links between groups. Another 220 possible links do not have decisions. The full source list has 2,358 exact name leads, so the index is not complete.

entries.title: Map credits move into the site interface
paragraphs: The live atlas removed the fixed Santiago coastline notice. A start-up credit and a permanent Map credits control now carry OpenStreetMap, ODbL, and Natural Earth attribution. This release has 438 cases across 448 playback stops. At that date, 176 known cases still needed text. Another 62 cases had holds. The update did not change the 676-event statistical release.

entries.title: Project updates and RSS
paragraphs: The project now has an Updates page and an RSS feed. Each post has its own address. The archive shows the work date and the date we added the post. These posts give information about live releases and decisions about the project. Older posts use project records that have dates.

entries.title: Next search plan
paragraphs: We agreed on the next search plan. First, we will join the accepted group records in one index. Then we will examine which searches apply and do a test of how we choose the next search. Each work cycle must cover all periods that still need searches. New finds at the end of a search start a short follow-up with a stated scope. Checks of search results use a repeatable sample and expand when they find errors.

entries.title: Matching play buttons
paragraphs: The start screen now has two play buttons of the same size. Their arrows point in opposite directions. Their labels line up. The layout is correct on wide and narrow screens. The change keeps the same cases and playback order.

entries.title: Play controls and sound
paragraphs: The play controls are in one bar. Site links are below the timeline. The sound keeps one key within a region. The key changes when the region changes. The atlas still has 533 cases and 543 stops.

entries.title: New report: discovery status
paragraphs: A new dated report shows the current discovery search and its limits. It lists 1,280 saved search records. Of these, 24 contain located results, 19 contain no result in scope, and 17 have evidence or access limits.

The current cycle has 19 partial search attempts across eight era blocks. No block meets the full search floor. The first test recovered zero of three eligible pairs. Three other pairs were outside the source scope. Source gaps do not rule out faults in the search prompts or source selection.
This report does not add atlas cases. The live atlas remains at 533 cases and 543 stops.

entries.title: New public case: Tawergha
paragraphs: The atlas adds the forced removal of Tawergha residents from their town in Libya in 2011. The case follows barriers to return and later return through 2025. Return did not mean full recovery.
The case keeps unknown values where the sources do not support a score or a map route. The atlas now contains 534 cases and 544 stops. There are 78 known ordinary cases left and 64 separate holds.
The dated discovery report keeps its earlier counts and search limits. This case update does not change that report or the frozen statistical release.

entries.title: Congo case and research updates
paragraphs: The atlas adds a case on refugee camp clearance in Congo in 1996 to 1997. The case separates deaths, forced flight, and return. The total number of affected people remains unknown.
The atlas now contains 535 cases and 545 stops. There are 77 known ordinary cases left and 64 separate holds.

The research ledger adds two Cameroon candidates: Bamum village expulsion and Ncharé conquest with land allocation. Their relation to one campaign remains unknown. A separate Tikar and Tumu lead lacks evidence of a land or residence loss. None of these records adds a public atlas case.
The separate statistical test now has five added events. The first comparison is due at 30 added events. The active statistical release still contains 676 events.
The updated discovery report lists search results and open questions. It does not claim a global coverage percentage.

entries.title: Flight and refuge in the Moriori case
paragraphs: The Moriori case now has a note on flight and refuge. It covers the history of Ngāti Tama and Ngāti Mutunga. The note describes warfare pressure in Taranaki and later moves toward Rēkohu.
A link leads to the source and its limits. The account does not show that every traveller fled. The case keeps its account of the invasion, deaths, enslavement, and land loss.

entries.title: Korean War civilian displacement added
paragraphs: The atlas now includes Korean War civilian displacement from 1950 to 1953. The case keeps summer flight and the winter retreat as distinct waves. It also separates refugees from North Korea from South Korean evacuees.

The source supports flight, limits on return, and new places of residence. It does not give one total for all people who moved. It also does not show one route, general title loss, or permanent exile for every civilian. Damaged number tables are not used.

links.label: Read Kim, sections II–IV and Conclusions, pages 285–329

entries.title: Maʻafu’s conquest and land reorganization in Lau added
paragraphs: The atlas now includes Maʻafu’s conquest and land changes in Lau from 1852 to 1869. The case has three phases. It covers war, changed rule, and measured land plots in named Lauan islands.

The sources show new tax and tribute ties. They also show plots for tax-paying men and some Tongan residents and warriors. They do not show that all residents left or that all land was seized. The number displaced, death share, and full land loss remain unknown.
The map uses regional context. Exact event geometry is unknown. Mago and Munia or Yanuyanu remain separate research leads. This atlas case is separate from the 676 active events.

links.label: Read Spurway, chapter 5 and Appendix G
Read the British Commissioners’ report, paragraphs 57–58

entries.title: Almoravid deportation in 1126 added
paragraphs: The atlas now includes the Almoravid deportation of Andalusi Christians to the Maghreb in 1126. The case covers named groups. These groups include families and church leaders. It does not cover every Christian in the named cities.

The account describes an order, armed pursuit, and legal actions after removal. A separate record concerns a church and its endowment. The full number displaced remains unknown. The sources do not establish a complete route or a replacement population.
The atlas has 538 cases and 550 stops. The sources have three links in the case. The active statistical release remains 676 events.

links.label: View the public data and source uses

Delfina Serrano, ‘Dos fetuas sobre la expulsión de mozárabes al Magreb en 1126,’ Anaquel de Estudios Árabes 2 (1991): 163–182. Order and named groups: pp. 167–168; Seville, Meknes, armed pursuit, post-removal sale requests and legal procedures: pp. 174–176; church and endowment record: pp. 170–173.

Alejandro García Sanjuán, ‘Declive y extinción de la minoría cristiana en la Sevilla andalusí (ss. XI–XII),’ Historia. Instituciones. Documentos 31 (2004): 269–286. Lost original opinion: p. 280; post-removal sale permission and procedure: p. 283; enforcement, selective removal and later institutional change: pp. 281–286.

Tarek Ladjal, ‘The Christian Presence in North Africa under Almoravid Rule (1040–1147 CE): Coexistence or Eradication?’ Cogent Arts & Humanities 4 (2017), 1334374, section 3.3. The count remains vague; later figures measure different groups.

entries.title: Kazakh flight and land loss, 1929–1934
paragraphs: The atlas adds a case on flight, forced returns and land loss in Kazakhstan from 1929 to 1934. State plans sought settled life, but many plans failed. The account keeps those plans separate from forced returns, local expulsions and pasture loss.

Pianciola argues that famine caused dependence and some settlement. He rejects violent settlement as the usual cause of the famine. He estimates that one-third of Kazakhs died in 1930–1933. The drop in the republic's Kazakh population also includes migration. These measures are separate. The sources do not give one total for people forced to move.

All eight trait values remain from the fixed model. Each has a source qualification. Filled cells show coding completion, not source confidence. The active statistical roster still has 676 events. The atlas has 539 cases and 551 stops.

links.label: View the public data and source uses
Niccolò Pianciola, Famine in the steppe (2004), pp. 137–138, 147, 154–156, 163–165, 170–181 and 186. Failed plans, flight, forced return, local expulsion, pasture loss and continued returns.
Niccolò Pianciola, Ukraine and Kazakhstan: Comparing the Famines (2018), pp. 441–442. Famine and partial settlement; attributed one-third mortality, separate death-plus-migration decline.

entries.title: Slave transport, contract work and island residence
paragraphs: The atlas adds a case on slave transport, contract work and residence in the Mascarenes and Seychelles. It spans 1638 to about 1920. The sources describe selected groups and periods. They do not show that every arrival was forced.

Two links show selected voyages in 1770 and 1807. The points are approximate place references. The arcs are not ship tracks. The departure port for the 1718 arrival in Bourbon is not mapped. Other routes and later fates remain unknown.

Slave transport and contract work remain separate. Some former workers bought small plots. The sources do not give one total for people forced to move, or deaths across this whole case. All eight fixed trait values and the family remain unchanged. Each trait has a source note.
The atlas has 540 cases and 552 stops. The active statistical roster still has 676 events. Eleven separate scientific entries remain inactive. The site keeps all 22 earlier update posts.

links.label: Open the Mascarene and Seychelles case
View public data and source uses

Richard B. Allen, “The Mascarenes, Indian Ocean Africa, and Global Labor Migration during the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries,” in African Islands (2019), pp. 294–316, DOI 10.1017/9781787444874.011. Only the official Summary, paragraphs 1–2, was read; the full chapter was not acquired.

Yadhav Deerpaul, Alexander Springer and Philip Gooding, “The first recorded outbreak of epidemic dropsy, 1877–80: Climate, empire, and colonial medical science between India, Bengal, and Mauritius,” Medical History 68(4) (2024), pp. 436–456, DOI 10.1017/mdh.2024.24. Contracts and estate placement: pp. 443–444; former-worker landholding: pp. 444–445; returnee recruitment: pp. 447–448; work and medical control: pp. 451–452. Epidemic estimates are not this case’s death count.

Rafaël Thiebaut, “Traite des esclaves malgaches à Bourbon,” Musée de Villèle, Portail de l’esclavage à La Réunion. See “L’histoire de la traite,” the 1718 expedition and Courrier de Bourbon paragraphs, note 6; “État des bâtiments entrés,” Action/Tamatave/4 May 1807 row; “Les particularités de la traite”; “La situation à Bourbon”; and “Les chiffres.” The essay uses mediated archives and historical scholarship.

Tony Mathiot, “250 Years Anniversary,” Seychelles National Museum (2020). See the opening voyage and passenger-list paragraphs, followed by the paragraphs on the 1771 move to Mahé and Romainville’s 1778 arrival. The list identifies seven African slaves; the status of five Indians and Marie is not stated. A secondary museum account, not an inspected passenger register.

entries.title: Source questions now visible
paragraphs: The research list now names source leads and cases that still need map locations. Each entry states what a source supports and what remains unknown.
The list also states the next step. Some cases already appear in the atlas. Their wider source questions remain open.
The new page adds no scores or map routes. The atlas cases and statistical release do not change.

entries.title: More source questions from India and Illinois
paragraphs: The source list now includes a royal land grant from southern India and two Illinois settlement studies.
The charter reports a loss of land rights. The Illinois studies do not establish forced departure or land loss.
Each entry states what remains unknown and what evidence is needed next. These research entries add no cases to the live atlas.

entries.title: New source questions from Nepal and Utah
paragraphs: The source list adds two entries from Nepal and Utah.
The Nepal entry is a candidate, with no scores. A royal text reports conquest of the city of the Mallas. Its date and modern site remain unknown.
The Utah entry concerns a possible refuge at Rock Island. It does not establish forced departure or land loss.
Neither entry adds a case to the live atlas. Unknown harm does not mean no harm.

entries.title: New source questions from Jebel Sahaba and a royal charter
paragraphs: The source list adds three entries. One concerns the Jebel Sahaba study. Two concern a royal charter from Udayendiram.
The Jebel Sahaba study reports repeated violence. The evidence reviewed here does not establish lost homes, forced flight or land loss.
The charter reports loss of prior land rights for a village grant. It also reports the defeat of a chief and rule over a district.
An order does not show that the chief left. The dates and the fate of residents remain unknown.
The Malla source assessment is done. Its next step is an atlas draft. These changes add no case to the live atlas.

entries.title: Burned homes and open source questions
paragraphs: The source list now includes Duckfoot in southwest North America. The author argues that someone burned the homes on purpose. He proposes that residents did this before they left. The cause of departure remains unknown.

The Whistling Elk entry adds an original field report. Excavators found a burned inner roof, a mostly unburned outer roof and floor objects. The authors infer a hasty departure. They propose an attack as one possible cause.
The Seminole entry now uses the same evidence rule as other entries. It seeks a bounded process and a land outcome for an affected group or tract. A named surviving community is not required.
These changes add no case to the live atlas.

entries.title: Two open questions on language and land
paragraphs: The source list adds a view from Golla. He suggests a Wintuan spread based on language patterns. The link to a forced move or land loss remains unknown. The linked Maiduan question stays open.
A separate entry covers Chilula encroachment on Wiyot land near Blue Lake. Golla reports a language boundary that moved west. The local effect on homes or land control remains unknown.
The wider account of land loss is not proof of this local outcome. The excerpt ends mid-section. These entries add no case to the live atlas.

entries.title: Two reports raise questions on camps and a town
paragraphs: The source list adds a published Tlingit oral account. It reports forced capture, ruined camps and property, and freer use of places to camp. Spirit stories form part of the account. The date and the event to assess remain open.
A royal text reports that a king ploughed down Pithumda with asses. This named-town claim remains unverified. The effects on residents, land rights and length of control are unknown.
Both entries state what the sources report and what remains unknown. They add no case to the live atlas.

entries.title: The Pithumda source assessment is saved
paragraphs: The source assessment of a royal report about Pithumda is saved. The text reports that a king ploughed the town. It does not confirm that the act took place.
Effects on residents, land rights and length of control remain unknown. The exact place and date are still unknown.
The source entry now gives the next step. This update adds no case to the live atlas and makes no change to active analysis.

entries.title: Three Sri Lanka research notes
paragraphs: Three research notes are now on the public list. Two concern reported changes of rule in Sri Lanka. One concerns a report that a group fled a threat to the life of its leader.
The chronicle calls both new regimes just. It does not show who lost homes or rights to land in the two takeovers. The threat to the leader does not prove that each person faced the same threat.
These are open research questions. They add no stop to the atlas and change no model score. The dates and wider effects on residents remain unclear.

entries.title: Three questions from a Zuni account
paragraphs: Three source questions are now on the public list. They come from the 1896 English account by Cushing.

The account reports a mountain-town defeat and a later group departure. It also reports that Winter clans fought into a valley and settled there. The third note covers its report of flight from Hanhlipinkya before destruction.
The dates and exact places remain unknown. The account does not prove that these acts took place. These notes add no atlas case or model score.

entries.title: Two questions from an Alaska report
paragraphs: Two source questions are now on the public list. They come from a 2018 state report on Alaska.

The report says a migration with Denbigh culture displaced or replaced earlier people. That choice stays open. It also describes Ipiutak injuries and later replacement. It does not link those injuries to a forced loss of homes or land.
These are open source questions. The report gives no firm event dates or modern group identity. The notes add no atlas case or scientific admission.

entries.title: Great Lakes source questions
paragraphs: 31 source questions from the Great Lakes region are now on the public list. They concern changes in rule, forced moves, land rights, and refuge.
The notes state what the source reports and what remains unknown. Some accounts report a move. Others leave its cause or result open. These questions add no atlas case or model score.
Two older notes now ask for more evidence after their source assessments.

entries.title: Bengal source questions
paragraphs: 10 source questions from a chapter on Bengal are now on the public list. Three are candidate hypotheses. Seven are leads with source locations.
These are open questions, not 10 confirmed cases. The notes state what the source reports and what remains unknown. Links to inactive profiles do not confirm that the reported events took place.
These questions add no public atlas case or model score.

entries.title: A Driftless research lead
paragraphs: We added one research note on villages and later moves in the Driftless Area. The authors propose that scarce resources and war helped drive these changes. The cause of each move remains open.
This note adds no atlas case or model score.

entries.title: Search report update
paragraphs: We updated the discovery report. It lists 60 known ordinary cases left in the local data.
The dated report shows the search gaps and open questions. It keeps inactive archive records separate from public atlas cases. The atlas itself did not change.

entries.title: Seven new research notes
paragraphs: We added seven research notes. One concerns reported Ho-Chunk removal from Wisconsin. Six concern reports of movement, land grants and rule in Bengal and nearby areas.
These notes state what each source supports and what remains unknown. They add no atlas case or score.

entries.title: Early North America: seven new notes
paragraphs: The research list adds seven notes on early eastern North America. It also updates the Midsouth note.
The notes cover claims of captives and disputes over site use. They also cover changes in homes. Each note states the source claims and limits.
We read six chapters and the shared reference list in one book. The cited field studies remain unread. These notes add no atlas cases.

entries.title: American Bottom note adds a field report
paragraphs: The American Bottom note now cites the original field report. We read 158 selected pages, not the full 490-page report.
At Sprague, part of a house pit filled with soil before a fire. The report suggests that people returned and reused homes and food stores. This does not prove that someone forced people to leave.
Wasps can nest in homes that people still use. The causes of local moves and earlier land use remain open.

entries.title: Chola source note and search scope update
paragraphs: One new note covers orders for temple staff from Chola villages. Texts 69 and 70 list pay and tax duties. Text 57 adds guard duties. The sources do not show if each order was carried out.

We also corrected the search record for 19 cells. We reopened 16 cells because earlier searches did not cover the full date span. Three cells now state limits on the search scope. We kept the earlier source results.
These changes add no case to the atlas. The map still has 540 cases and 552 stops. More work on early North America and South Asia remains open.

entries.title: Northeast research notes
paragraphs: We added seven research notes for Northeast North America. They cover village moves, forced departures and a disputed migration model.
We also checked the Sirkap note against the text by Marshall. He assigns quake damage to one layer. He places another layer after conquest. The cause of later damage remains open.
These research updates add no case to the map or model. The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops.

entries.title: New source notes on the lower Indus
paragraphs: We added four source notes and revised the Saka note. Puri reports a forced Saka move toward the lower Indus. The new notes also cover two tales and a land gift.
The Minnagara note concerns princes who repeatedly lost rule. The translated report does not show physical removal of princes or residents. The record stays inactive.
The tales do not establish that each reported act took place. We still need to assess the effects of the land gift. The fate of prior residents remains unknown.
These notes add no atlas case or model score. The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops.
An archive of the earlier site is now available. The concept DOI links the archived versions. The GitHub repository has the current public snapshot. New site notes do not alter the earlier archive.

entries.title: Assam and Baikal source notes
paragraphs: We added nine source notes: three on Assam and six on the Baikal area. They ask how rule, flight and new arrivals changed control of land.
The Assam notes cover early Ahom conquest, later conquests and loss of rule. They keep these periods apart. The accounts do not establish forced moves by prior residents.

The Baikal notes cover flight from troops, forced return and land disputes. They also ask how new arrivals put pressure on prior residents. The source is a student essay that retells stories with few source details. Separate events remain unproved.

We revised two Alaska notes. The report of injuries does not by itself prove who caused later changes. Results from farther east do not settle these Alaska questions. Parts of the Cape report are now read. The source questions remain open.
These notes add no atlas case or model score. The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops.

entries.title: Pushkalavati and Alaska source notes
paragraphs: A note by Beal reports a siege and the loss of rule at Pushkalavati. The fate of the people, the exact site and the date remain unclear.

Two Alaska notes now include more site evidence. The Cape Krusenstern report describes homes, food storage and a burned house with the remains of three people. It does not show what caused the fire or link it to forced removal.
A new research record holds the city claim and its limits. It is outside the fitted model. The atlas case count and model results are unchanged.

entries.title: Two Bhir source questions
paragraphs: Two new research notes concern Bhir Mound at Taxila. Marshall reports a Greek sack. He thinks the West Group fire probably took place at that time. That link remains uncertain. The possible end of use of this tract remains a question.

Marshall also describes walls that blocked lanes and stopped public shortcuts. The account does not establish the loss of a prior public right. It does not establish a forced move. These research notes add no atlas case or model score.

entries.title: A reported Tlingit fort loss
paragraphs: A published Tlingit oral account reports an attack on Murrelet-point fort and the capture of women there. This fort loss now has a separate research note. The broad war account stays separate.
The date, modern site and modern groups remain unknown. The account does not set a date before 1000. This note does not confirm the event through an independent source.
The Bhir note still treats the reported sack and probable fire link as uncertain. These research notes add no atlas case or model score.

entries.title: Four new notes on rights and home loss
paragraphs: Four new research notes cover Sonpur, eastern Wisconsin, Norris Farms and Etowah. They add records of reported loss of rights, homes or village use.
Dalton reports that Singrai Manki lost rights and control over 12 villages in Sonpur. This does not establish that all residents left. The date of the loss remains unknown.
Dye reports that Oneota groups drove local groups out or absorbed them in eastern Wisconsin. The cause of the Aztalan departure remains uncertain.
At Norris Farms, Dye reports attacks, flight and a later return. He does not establish permanent loss of the village.
Dye reports that people left Etowah. A severe attack is one possible cause. The Crow Creek note keeps the fire link and later village use uncertain.
These four notes and the Crow Creek correction add no atlas case or model score. The 80 archive records remain inactive.

entries.title: New next steps for four research notes
paragraphs: Four research notes now keep each reported account as one research record. Their next steps retain the open questions.
Puri reports a forced Saka move toward the lower Indus. Other routes and the fate of prior residents remain open. His account does not show that residents lost their land.
Dye reports that Oneota groups drove local groups out or absorbed them in eastern Wisconsin. The cause of the Aztalan departure remains uncertain.
At Norris Farms, Dye reports attacks, flight and a later return. He does not establish permanent loss of the village.
At Crow Creek, Dye describes an attack and apparent flight. The fire link and later village use remain uncertain.
The three North America notes share one Dye source family. The Saka note uses one Puri synthesis. These status changes add no atlas case or model score. They do not complete a region or era.

entries.title: Four Sri Lanka research notes
paragraphs: Four Sri Lanka research notes now join the source list. Two use a study by Deraniyagala. Two use the Mahavamsa chronicle.

The study links Iron Age arrivals with Nagas as a reconstruction. Local change remains an alternative. It also links wet-rice growth with pressure on Yakka and Vadda life. Coexistence and retained identity remain part of that account.

The chronicle reports the siege and destruction of Vijitanagara. It also says people fled from the river bank to that city. Their mix and later fate remain unknown. The siege does not settle the fate of those people.
These four questions add no atlas case or model score. They do not verify loss totals or complete a region or era.
This work took place on October 16 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Four Great Basin research notes
paragraphs: Four Great Basin research notes now join the source list. Two remain located questions. Two are candidates for further review.
Kroeber infers western Mono settlement from shared speech. His account gives no date or land seizure. We keep that question apart from the broad Numic spread case.
The Owens Valley Indian Water Commission describes forced removal to Fort Tejon and return. Its account also describes land loss and ranch labor. This question overlaps the broad California case.
Its account also describes Los Angeles land and water purchases. Which Native homes or land uses those purchases displaced remains unclear.

A separate note covers a land exchange in the 1930s. The source reports a smaller occupied land base. Proposals for moves outside the valley do not establish actual moves. The source gives 1937 and 1939. Consent and force remain unresolved.
These four research entries add no playable case or model score. They do not settle dates, counts or the extent of loss.
This work took place on October 16 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Three Talagunda research notes and one Owens Valley update
paragraphs: Three Talagunda research notes join the source list. One is a candidate for review of a reported grant of land. Two remain located questions.
The translated royal praise poem says Pallava rulers made Mayurasarman a friend. He served them, then received land under a pact. The scope of control and the Prehara boundary remain unknown.

A separate note concerns his base in a forest. Kielhorn links its place name to Srisaila. That link is an editor inference. The forest is not known to match the later grant. The dates and any loss for prior residents remain unknown.

The third note concerns kin who sought refuge in Kakustha territory. The poem says stronger parties harassed them. Shelter alone does not establish a forced move or a loss of land for earlier residents.
The Owens Valley note keeps forced removal and return as one research record. The death toll and terms of labor remain unknown.
These notes add no playable case or model score. The royal praise account does not by itself establish land loss in all three Talagunda accounts.
This work took place on October 16 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Crow Creek: an original source account and its limits
paragraphs: The Crow Creek source note now includes the original thesis by Willey. This is an update to the same research record.
Willey describes an attack and burned lodges. He concludes that the village lost its use as a home, fortress and social center.
He considers that some people escaped. He proposes that escaped villagers or people with ties to them came to bury the dead. He also reports later ceremonies at the site.
The attackers and all survivor destinations remain unknown. The fire dates and later use of the village as homes remain uncertain.
We read the full site and interpretation sections, with front matter and references. The detailed methods in other chapters remain unread.
The thesis is one source account. Its cited works do not count as separate sources read for this update.
This account adds no playable case or model score. It does not establish permanent vacancy or land gain by the attackers. It does not fill the early North America gap.
This work took place on October 17 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Known but not yet placeable: a guide to the research list
paragraphs: Known but not yet placeable is the public list of research questions. It draws from the project ledger. Each entry names a place and a time span.
Each source entry states what the evidence supports, what remains unknown and the next step. It links to the sources. Some entries are leads. Others have a reviewed source account.
A place on this list is not admission to the atlas roster. It is not a conclusion of forced removal or a model score. A record can stay open or leave the candidate queue after review.
Unknown evidence does not mean no harm. The list is not a census of harm or proof that the project found every case.
The page also lists cases that await map locations in a separate section. Those cases already belong to the atlas. Their place limits differ from the open research questions.
The Discovery link in the atlas opens the search report. That report links to this list. The link below opens the list.
This update also repairs marker colors and adds a key. The map keeps the same cases and data.
This work took place on October 17 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Peter Village and two South Asian accounts
paragraphs: The same three research notes now state their source limits. They cover Peter Village and two accounts from South Asia.
Clay places Peter Village in Fayette County, Kentucky. Dye places the Peter enclosure in northwestern Ohio. This conflict remains open.
Clay reports post holes, burned wood, a ditch and an inner bank. These traces alone do not establish forced departure or lost access.
At Talagunda in India, the translated praise poem reports a grant of land to Mayurasarman. Its use and effects on prior users remain unknown.
The Mahavamsa says the king took Vijitanagara in a siege and destroyed the city. This account concerns Sri Lanka. The date, exact site and fate of residents remain unknown.
The chronicle has a heroic and religious frame. Its religious speech devalues the dead. It also gives grief, restraint and rites for Elara.
Its last verse condemns deaths from greed. Its large totals lack a verified count.
These notes add no playable case or model score. They do not close the gaps in early North America, South Asia or all eras.
This work took place on October 17 in Denver time. This post dates to October 17 in UTC.

entries.title: Four new research notes
paragraphs: New notes cover Gallina, Nasik and Embobut Forest. One more asks about the coastal shell rings of North America.
Each note states what the source supports and what is unknown. The Ahom entry also changed after review.
These are research notes, not new atlas cases. The case count and model results stay the same.

entries.title: Eight research notes from Bengal and the Kurils
paragraphs: Eight research notes are new. Seven concern Bengal. One concerns a forced move from the northern Kurils to Shikotan.
The Bengal notes cover three reported exiles, a town capture and a temple site. Two more ask about settlement and a crop levy. Each note states its source limits.
These notes do not add eight cases to the atlas. The live atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops.

entries.title: Six Bengal research notes
paragraphs: Six research notes are new. Four ask about reported conquests in Bengal and nearby lands. Two ask about rules for noble homes and property.
The conquest notes concern Kaikaus, Fakhr al-Din, Sikandar and Jalal al-Din. The source reports changes in control. It does not establish every local effect.
The source also reports rules for nobles who had to live in the capital and property that passed back to the ruler. Their dates remain unknown.
These are source questions, not six new atlas cases. The live atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops.

entries.title: Notes on Hirakud and Kaikaus
paragraphs: One new research note concerns homes and fields at Hirakud in India. The book reports state-led moves as water covered land near Sambalpur. It gives figures for 1954-55 and a summer 1955 start. Those dates do not fix the last move.

The book also reports plans to flood some land in Madhya Pradesh. It does not show full payment or new land for all people. Some buyers got less land as prices rose. Land rights and later returns stay unclear.

The Kaikaus note now has a new next step: prepare the case for the atlas. Eaton reports a conquest in southeast Bengal, dated to 1291, and a change in rule. The local rights and the fate of the people remain unknown.
These notes are part of research work. They add no new stops to the live atlas.
We also read the full Rock Island report from southeast Utah. Matson and Morin interpret the site as a place for homes and defense. A forced move and loss of home land stay unresolved.

entries.title: Two Ho research notes
paragraphs: Two new notes concern land use in the Seraikella area of India. A report from 1927 draws on fieldwork in 1925. The event dates remain unknown.

One note concerns a burial ground at Paharpur. The authors say the Mundri clan took control of a site once linked to the Haiburu clan. They say the site no longer allowed Haiburu burial. How it changed hands remains unknown.

The other note concerns a State ban on tree use. The authors say the State did not allow the Ho to cut trees. They link a lack of firewood to a shift from cremation to burial. The start date, reach and enforcement of the ban remain unknown.
Both notes ask how to assess lost land use. Neither establishes eviction or loss of homes. They add no new stops to the live atlas.

entries.title: Homes at Hulas
paragraphs: One new research note concerns homes at Hulas in northern India. Excavators found homes, hearths and rebuilt floors.

The report places later homes north of an earlier settlement. It does not state why use of the old homes ended. It does not establish forced removal or explain how later people came to use nearby land.
The note records an open question. It adds no stop to the live atlas.

entries.title: Three new research notes
paragraphs: Three new research notes concern Sirsukh in Pakistan and two sites in Fiji. They record open questions, not new stops in the atlas.
Marshall says Kushan rulers left Sirkap and built a new walled city at Sirsukh. The account does not establish a loss of prior land use or control. Forced moves from Sirkap remain unproven.
At Volivoli II, the authors infer repeated shelter use with breaks. The deposits do not show why use stopped or whether people lost access.
The Ugaga account reports a land gift around 1830 in return for defence. It does not establish which prior rights changed. Later claims from 1997 do not settle rights today.

entries.title: North America: new research notes
paragraphs: We added 13 research notes and revised three earlier notes. They cover reported attacks, village loss and land recovery in North America. Each note states what the source records and what still needs proof. These notes do not add cases to the atlas.

entries.title: Barrie note and research report
paragraphs: We added a research note on Barrie village and refreshed the dated discovery report. Sutton argues that migrants founded the village. The note keeps the date conflict and gaps in earlier land use visible. It does not establish a forced move. The atlas has no new case.

entries.title: Two research questions from southern India
paragraphs: We added two research notes on southern India. One tracks changes in hilltop villages. The other asks how people changed shared places and water access. The study does not establish forced removal. Atlas case totals stay the same.

entries.title: Later homes near Cahokia
paragraphs: We added two research notes on later Indigenous homes near Cahokia. One concerns renewed use near Horseshoe Lake. The other concerns a reported move in 1735 under pressure from French colonists.
The study also reports later forced moves to Oklahoma. A possible later departure and the forced moves remain separate research questions. Atlas case totals stay the same.

entries.title: Nine notes on homes and departures
paragraphs: We added eight research notes from the book by Bahr on O'odham accounts. They describe homes, war, escape, captives, new homes and peace. The accounts have different tellers and versions. Their event dates remain unknown.

We also added a National Park Service note on Antelope Creek. It describes homes, farms, flint use and later departure. Drought or pressure and attacks are possible causes. Forced clearance remains unproven.
The dated report now lists 304 source notes and 151 map notes. These nine notes add no atlas cases or active model scores.

entries.title: Three notes on homes and war
paragraphs: We added three notes on Moundville and the Black Warrior River valley. They draw on one chapter by Knight and Steponaitis. These are research questions, not new atlas cases or active model scores.

The first note describes a new town with walls and a planned layout. Builders cleared earlier structures for it. People moved inside the walls. The account does not establish forced moves or the expulsion of prior users.

The next note covers homes that became grave sites after about 1300. The authors propose three possible causes for the move from the center. Leaders sought a more sacred center, local soils and wood ran short, or the threat of attack fell. The authors do not choose one cause. The causes can act together.

The last note covers the loss of valley residents about 1650. The authors link that loss to war pressure across the region. The account does not show what happened to all residents. It establishes neither a death toll nor new settlers.
The dated report lists 307 source notes and 151 map notes. The feed has 69 posts. The live atlas remains at 540 cases and 552 stops.

entries.title: Six new notes on land and homes
paragraphs: We added six research notes on Hastinapura from one report by Lal. They cover land grants, fire and reuse, a later settlement, and accounts that Lal cites. Each note links to the report. These are research questions, not new atlas cases or active model scores.

Lal reports land grants to displaced people and former servicemen. He also describes homes after a fire, plus later homes and glazed pots. The notes keep those accounts separate. They do not infer forced moves from the finds alone.

Other notes cover accounts of a kingdom, exile and a change of capital. Lal compares some of these accounts with the finds. Those links remain tentative. An account in a text does not by itself prove that the events took place.
The list now has 313 source notes and 151 map notes. The feed has 70 posts. The live atlas stays at 540 cases and 552 stops. The dated report also keeps local research apart from the live atlas.

entries.title: A note on homes and access at Sisupalgarh
paragraphs: We added a research note on homes and access at Sisupalgarh. Lal reports that people lived there before the fort walls. The report describes walls, gates, roads and homes, with repairs and later use.

A brick wall later closed a side passage. The reason and the effects on prior users remain unknown. The report does not establish that these acts forced people from their land or homes. The note links to the report in its original issue.

The list now has 314 source notes and 151 map notes. The feed has 71 posts. The live atlas stays at 540 cases and 552 stops. This note adds a research question, not a new atlas case or an active model score.

entries.title: Two notes on moves near the Saint Lawrence
paragraphs: We prepared two research questions on 18 October. We added their notes on 19 October. One concerns Jefferson County around 1500. The other concerns later moves from the Saint Lawrence valley.

The authors propose that some groups built new communities or joined other groups. Pottery links trace changes in contact between sites. These links do not count migrants or show that force caused each move. Conflict remains a proposed cause.
The list now has 316 source notes and 151 map notes. The feed has 72 posts. The live atlas stays at 540 cases and 552 stops. These notes add no atlas cases or active model scores.

entries.title: New notes on flight, exile and rule
paragraphs: We added 19 notes to Known but not yet placeable. Two concern movements in the Mesa Verde region. Seventeen come from texts and comments in the 1884 edition by Samuel Beal.
The Beal notes describe reported flight, exile, changes of rule and the purchase of people for service. Several accounts are tales. Dates and links between some accounts remain unclear.
Each note sets out what the source reports, what remains unknown and the next research question. These are research notes. They do not add atlas cases or change the statistical results.

entries.title: Ten research notes on Mesa Verde and Hopi accounts
paragraphs: We added ten research notes about the Mesa Verde region and Hopi accounts. They cover reported violence, departures, access to land, help from hosts and continued use of settlements.
Each new note gives the source, chapter and printed pages. It states what the evidence supports and what remains unknown. We also clarified a date limit in one earlier note.
These notes are research questions. They do not add atlas cases or change the statistical results.

entries.title: Public files now omit private paths
paragraphs: The report uses record IDs and file hashes. We call the review the external audit.
Some public provenance files have new hashes compared with the archived originals. The case accounts, scores and calculations stay the same.

entries.title: 24 South Asia research notes with source links
paragraphs: We added 24 South Asia research notes. Each note has a source link and printed page locations. The notes cover royal flight, capture and conquest.
These notes draw on three works. One is an English translation. Two are articles that discuss older texts and inscriptions. These works share sources. They are not three independent witnesses.

Each note states what the source reports and what remains unknown. The effects on homes and land are still questions in some notes. These are research notes, not 24 new atlas cases. The atlas counts and statistical results stay the same.

entries.title: Four Arkansas research notes with source links
paragraphs: We added four Arkansas research notes from one chapter by Michael P. Hoffman. Two notes cover accounts of conflict. Two others follow leads on the loss of homes and the movement of survivors.
The notes keep the dates of recorded accounts distinct from the dates of events. Each note states what the chapter reports and what remains unknown. We did not read the older sources it cites.
The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 playback stops. These research notes do not add atlas cases or change the statistical results.

entries.title: 52 new research notes
paragraphs: We added 52 research notes to the discovery list. They include histories from North America, Angola, and parts of Asia.
These notes are research records. They are not new atlas cases. Each note states what the source supports, what remains unclear, and what we must examine next.
The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 playback stops. This update keeps the map notes and the earlier posts unchanged.

entries.title: Three new research notes
paragraphs: The research list adds notes on Jessore, Sand Canyon Pueblo and the territory Mahmud ceded to Sher Khan. Each note states what its source supports and what remains unknown. These records await atlas assessment.
The dated search report now records 54 partial attempts across 31 blocks and eight eras. Most search cells still await source work. No search channel, floor or cycle is complete.
The live atlas has 540 cases and 552 stops. The frozen release keeps its 676 events. The 104 separate scientific records remain inactive.

entries.title: Research notes on Bengal and early North America
paragraphs: Four new entries ask about early North America. One concerns moves into walled towns in East Tennessee. Two concern possible migration and refuge. The fourth concerns later use of Etowah. The earlier Etowah entry now keeps two source accounts distinct.
Manrique describes the seizure and sale of wives and children for unpaid taxes in Bengal. The link to loss of homes or land remains unresolved.
These are research entries, not new atlas cases. The migration and refuge ideas remain hypotheses. Each source note states what the evidence supports and what remains unknown.
The search report now logs 56 partial attempts in 31 blocks across eight eras. No search channel or cycle is complete.

entries.title: New research notes on North America and South Asia
paragraphs: This update adds 97 research notes and revises eight older notes. The new notes include early North America and South Asia. These are research questions, not new atlas cases.
At Saunaktuk, authors link human bones from a house site to a local account of an attack. That link remains uncertain. An estimate for use of the site does not date the attack.

At Orendorf, Wilson reports burned homes and a hurried departure. He identifies warfare as the most likely cause. A letter from 1827 reports that Limbu and Lepcha families fled to forest camps near the Nepal-Sikkim frontier. The exact flight dates remain unknown.
Revised notes add original-source references and state what those sources do not establish. The atlas still has 540 cases and 552 stops. All 151 map notes remain unchanged.
Read the notes for the evidence and open questions. The dated search report records partial searches, not global coverage.

entries.title: New research notes from India and Arctic Canada
paragraphs: The list now has eight new notes from India. They cover land grants, control of forts and forced removal. These notes record candidates and leads for research. They are not new cases in the atlas.

The Saunaktuk note sets out the authors' interpretation of resident deaths and loss of homes. Some bone marks can reflect acts after death. They do not prove how each person died. The attack date, attackers and fate of other residents remain unknown.
Read the notes in Known but not yet placeable.
